Block Party

Give residents a way to shape their neighborhood

Explore a place, propose a change, and stay part of the conversation.

  • Civic design
  • Participatory research
  • Spatial interaction

Block Party began as my HCI/d capstone at Indiana University Bloomington. I explored how civic-oriented residents aged 18–35 could understand urban proposals and contribute ideas before decisions were made.

The current browser prototype extends that concept with a categorized builder, proposal feedback, and progress updates.

6 residents tested the capstone prototype

They saw value in its potential for inclusive community engagement. This qualitative feedback applies to the 2025 prototype; the current app has no documented retest or measured participation increase.

A public meeting only works if people can take part.

My research in Bloomington pointed to low awareness of planning meetings, inconvenient participation methods, and proposals that were difficult to picture in context. Younger residents were often missing from the conversation.

I narrowed an initially broad urban-design problem to Bloomington community projects and residents aged 18–35. That focus made the concept specific enough to test.

Listen to both sides of participation.

The capstone combined secondary research and digital ethnography with resident and planning interviews. A participatory workshop helped explore three directions: a collaborative kiosk, an AR app, and a simulated neighborhood.

Paper concepts were also compared with 2 city planners and 2 users. These are activity-specific counts; participant overlap is unconfirmed.

See the place before judging the proposal.

I chose the simulation direction to bring exploration, feedback, and resident-made proposals into one experience. A map gives changes a spatial context; project details explain their purpose and constraints.

The current prototype pairs a project list with an illustrated, pannable city. Search, zoom, recenter, and a simulated street view support exploration. Sample project details leave unconfirmed dates, contacts, and dimensions explicit.

Give people a starting point for their ideas.

Prefabricated elements make it possible to suggest a use for a space without drawing a plan from scratch. The trade-off is a bounded set of choices, rather than a full design tool.

In the current app, residents browse Buildings, Outdoors, and Mobility, then drag an element onto the highlighted plot—or select and tap to place it. They can adjust or remove elements, save a draft, and review a name and description before a mock submission.

Keep participation going after “submit.”

A resident needs to know what happens to an idea. The revised prototype adds an acknowledgment, a reference number, a next step, and a progress tracker in Notifications. Updates are grouped around proposals the resident submitted, voted on, or commented on.

Separate proposal views support votes and discussion. Their sample counts show how the interface behaves; they do not establish community consensus or real planning decisions.

What testing revealed—and what still needs testing.

Six Bloomington residents tested the 2025 high-fidelity prototype. They saw it as a valuable, inclusive way to engage with community projects and identified two usability refinements.

Finding 01

Make elements easier to choose.

Participants needed clearer categories in the builder. The current app now groups elements by function; its effect on usability still needs testing.

Finding 02

Make the result easy to notice.

A proposed design’s arrival in the plot needed more emphasis. The current app provides placement feedback and a submission preview; whether these resolve the original issue is untested.

The original findings support the concept’s potential, not city-wide adoption or improved participation. The current interactive version is a later prototype, not the artifact tested in 2025.

An inviting interface is only part of inclusion.

Architecture taught me to think about how a place affects everyday life. This project pushed me to ask whose experience reaches a planning decision—and whose is missing.

Next, I would test the revised builder and progress flow with residents of different digital confidence levels, then work with planners on interpreting conflicting input. A digital channel needs outreach and a credible review process before it can represent a community.
